grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akavakwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akavakwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nemadzitateguru'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nemadzitateguru'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'madzitateguru' forms 'nemadzitateguru'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: The Passive Voice ('-wa' / '-iwa') in 'akavakwa'
grammar_notes.content: Notice how 'akavakwa' ends in '-wa' right before the final '-a'. In Shona, you turn an active verb into a passive verb ('is done / was done')  simply by inserting '-w-' (or '-iw-' / '-ew-') before the final vowel '-a'! For example: '-bika' (cook) becomes '-bikwa' ('be cooked', as in 'pakubikwa'), '-vaka' (build) becomes '-vakwa' ('be built'), '-ruma' (bite/sting) becomes '-rumwa' ('be stung', as in 'arumwa nenyuchi'), and '-zivikanwa' means 'be known'.
grammar_notes.rule: Verb Root + -wa / -iwa = Passive ('be [verb]-ed') -> -bika (cook) -> -bikwa (be cooked); -vaka (build) -> -vakwa (be built)

cultural_notes.title: The Mortarless Stone Engineering of Great Zimbabwe ('Masvingo eKare')
cultural_notes.content: Built by Shona ancestors ('madzitateguru edu') between 1100 and 1450 AD, the Great Enclosure at Great Zimbabwe features granite walls rising up to 11 metres high and 250 metres around, constructed from nearly a million hand-dressed granite blocks laid without a single drop of mortar ('matombo asina dhaka'). Its chevron wall patterns and conical tower remain marvels of African engineering.

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('anoti')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'anoti' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('mavara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'mavara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('matatu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'matatu' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

cultural_notes.title: Flag Colours, Design & the National Symbols of Zimbabwe
cultural_notes.content: Adopted at Independence on 18 April 1980, Zimbabwe's national flag ('mureza weZimbabwe') is rich in symbolism: green represents agriculture and the land's flora, yellow stands for mineral wealth (gold, platinum, and diamonds), red commemorates the blood shed for independence, black represents the heritage of the majority population, white symbolizes peace, and the soapstone Zimbabwe Bird ('Hungwe') connects the modern nation to Great Zimbabwe.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akagara')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akagara' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('maviri')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'maviri' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

cultural_notes.title: Donkey-Drawn Carts ('Ngoro yeMadhongi') in Rural Transport
cultural_notes.content: Across rural Zimbabwe—especially in drier regions—two-wheeled carts ('zvigochikari' or 'ngoro') pulled by pairs of hardy donkeys ('madhongi maviri') or oxen are indispensable for transporting grain sacks to the grinding mill ('chigayo'), firewood, and water drums along unpaved country roads ('mugwagwa usina tara').

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('Pasi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'Pasi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

cultural_notes.title: Zimbabwe's Trunk Highways & Seasonal Savannah Grass ('Sora Rakaoma')

During the dry winter and spring months from June to October, the roadside savannah grass ('sora') turns golden and dry ('rakaoma') beneath deep-rooted indigenous trees that stay green all year round.

sections.heading: 3. Cultural Context & Practical Usage
points: The Mortarless Stone Engineering of Great Zimbabwe ('Masvingo eKare'): Built by Shona ancestors ('madzitateguru edu') between 1100 and 1450 AD, the Great Enclosure at Great Zimbabwe features granite walls rising up to 11 metres high and 250 metres around, constructed from nearly a million hand-dressed granite blocks laid without a single drop of mortar ('matombo asina dhaka').

Flag Colours, Design & the National Symbols of Zimbabwe: Adopted at Independence on 18 April 1980, Zimbabwe's national flag ('mureza weZimbabwe') is rich in symbolism: green represents agriculture and the land's flora, yellow stands for mineral wealth (gold, platinum, and diamonds), red commemorates the blood shed for independence, black represents the heritage of the majority population, white symbolizes peace, and the soapstone Zimbabwe Bird ('Hungwe') connects the modern nation to Great Zimbabwe..

Donkey-Drawn Carts ('Ngoro yeMadhongi') in Rural Transport: Across rural Zimbabwe—especially in drier regions—two-wheeled carts ('zvigochikari' or 'ngoro') pulled by pairs of hardy donkeys ('madhongi maviri') or oxen are indispensable for transporting grain sacks to the grinding mill ('chigayo'), firewood, and water drums along unpaved country roads ('mugwagwa usina tara')..

Tropical Fruit Growing ('Chinanasi') in Zimbabwe's Eastern Highlands: Thanks to high rainfall, fertile red soils, and warm valleys in Manicaland's Rusitu Valley, Chipinge, and Honde Valley, Zimbabwe grows sweet tropical fruits ('michero') including pineapples ('zvinanasi'), bananas, avocados, macadamia nuts, and tea on lush mountain slopes..

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakarogedzwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakarogedzwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('Inosanganisira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'Inosanganisira' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('huchena')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'huchena'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('mitatu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'mitatu' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).

grammar_notes.content: The verb 'inoratidza' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('muchena')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'muchena'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).

grammar_notes.title: Connecting Clauses & Expressing Purpose with 'kuti'
grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'ndinoziva' = I know), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! For instance, '-dya' (eat) becomes 'kuti tidye' ('so that we may eat'), and '-wana' (get) becomes 'kuti uwane' ('so that you may get').
grammar_notes.rule: kuti + [Subject Prefix + Verb ending in -e] = 'so that [someone] may...' (e.g., kuti tidye = so that we eat)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('rakaiswawo')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'rakaiswawo' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

cultural_notes.content: On warm afternoons in Zimbabwe, welcoming a guest to the table with a cold glass of cordial—most famously Zimbabwe's iconic Mazoe Orange Crush diluted with chilled water and ice cubes ('magodo echando' from the 'firiji')—or a bottled soft drink ('chigubhu chedhiringi') is a beloved tradition of home hospitality.

Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('zvitatatu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'zvitatatu' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

cultural_notes.title: Rhino Conservation ('Zvipembere') in Zimbabwe's National Parks
cultural_notes.content: Zimbabwe is one of Southern Africa's most important strongholds for both the black and white rhinoceros ('chipembere', plural 'zvipembere'), protected in sanctuaries such as Matobo National Park, Hwange, and the Lowveld conservancies.

grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'maviri' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('Parutivi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'Parutivi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

cultural_notes.title: Homestead Garden Tools ('Maturusi') & Local Blacksmith Craftsmanship

sections.heading: 3. Cultural Context & Practical Usage
points: Fresh Market Produce ('Michero neMiriwo') & Healthy Nutrition: Zimbabwe's varied altitudes allow farmers to grow both temperate fruits like apples ('maapuro') from Nyanga in the Eastern Highlands and rich red tomatoes ('madomasi') and leafy greens ('miriwo') across the highveld, prized for strengthening immunity ('kurwisana nezvirwere mumuviri')..

Open-Air Clothing Markets ('Mabhero' / 'Kotamai') & Local Fashion: Across Zimbabwean towns and growth points, open-air clothing markets are popular places to shop for affordable, stylish garments ('mbatya' or 'hembe') and hats ('ngowani').

The Sitting Room ('Imba Yokutandarira') & Zimbabwean Wood & Stone Carvings: Literally meaning 'the room for relaxing and conversing together', the 'imba yokutandarira' is the pride of a Zimbabwean home.

Mining Tipper Trucks ('Rori Huru') & Zimbabwe's Great Dyke Mineral Belt: Heavy tipper trucks ('marori makuru anozvitutunura') are a familiar sight at mines ('kumamaini') along Zimbabwe's famous Great Dyke—a 550-kilometre geological feature holding some of the world's richest deposits of platinum, chrome, gold, and lithium..

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakachenuruka')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakachenuruka' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('ruvara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'ruvara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('mbiri')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'mbiri' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('vakawarira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'vakawarira' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pasi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pasi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

cultural_notes.title: Household Wares Markets & Woven Carrier Bags ('Mashangani')
cultural_notes.content: At bustling community markets, vendors spread out practical household goods—sun hats, clothes pegs ('mapegisi'), scrubbing brushes ('mabhurashi'), and basins. Shoppers carry their purchases home in colourful woven checkered carrier bags colloquially known across Southern Africa as 'mashangani' bags.

lessons.title: Chidzidzo 90: Musha wakapakwa mota yerudzi rutema, pane...
lessons.shona_text: Musha wakapakwa mota yerudzi rutema, pane muti wemupichisi une mashizha akasvibira uyewo pamusoro pejurahoro panoonekwa zvidhinha zvakarongwa zvakawandira mukati Motikari yakamira pamumugwagwa inozivikanwa ichinzi gonyeti.Ine musoro muhombe ine ruvara rutsvuku nesirivha.Pamhiri pari kuonekwa imba yakavakwa ichiita kunge mahofisi ine midhuri yeruvara rweorenji nezvichena nemiti iri kureba iri kumera ipapo.

sections.heading: 3. Cultural Context & Practical Usage
points: Veranda Container Gardening & Ornamental Plants in Zimbabwe: Container gardening—planting ornamental foliage and flowers ('maruva') in painted pots and tins ('magaba') arranged along smooth cement verandas ('pamusoro peuriri hwesimende')—is a cherished tradition in Zimbabwean homes, bringing greenery right to the doorstep even during the dry season..

Household Wares Markets & Woven Carrier Bags ('Mashangani'): At bustling community markets, vendors spread out practical household goods—sun hats, clothes pegs ('mapegisi'), scrubbing brushes ('mabhurashi'), and basins.

Springtime 'Kupfumvutira' of Indigenous Trees & School Stationery Shops: Notice the expressive verb 'kupfumvutira'—the bursting forth of fresh new leaves on roadside trees in spring (September–October), when Zimbabwe's 'musasa' trees flush in brilliant shades of bronze, crimson, and fresh green before the rains! Meanwhile, town shops ('zvitoro') stock up on books ('mabhuku'), pens ('zvinyoreso'), and glue for the school term..

Footwear Craftsmanship ('Shangu') & Bustling Town Walkways: Zimbabwe has a long tradition of leatherwork and footwear manufacturing (centered historically in Gweru with companies like Bata), alongside skilled roadside cobblers who keep leather shoes ('shangu') polished and repaired for busy city life..

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('rakatsvukuruka')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'rakatsvukuruka' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('runoita')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'runoita' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('yeruvara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'yeruvara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akagadzikwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.content: The verb 'anosanganisira' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('paneruvara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'paneruvara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).

lessons.title: Chidzidzo 95: Vanhu vakaungana mubani vese vane migomo...
lessons.shona_text: Vanhu vakaungana mubani vese vane migomo zvinove zvigubu zvekuratidza kuti varikucherera mvura parutivi pavo pane Jojo tengi rakavakirwa pamusoro rikatsveta pamusoro pechi mudhuri zvichiratidza kuti ndimo murikubva mvura yavari kuchereredza. Nzvimbo inemiti yakasiyana siyana inosanganisira muti wemumango. Muti wemumango una mashizha aneruvara rwegirinhi. Koita zvakare maruva aripedyo neruzhowa. Maruva aya anamashizha aneruvara rwegirinhi neruvara rwepingi. Mudzimai mutsvuku akashongedza kumeso kwake akanyora tsiye dzake zvakanaka akapenda kumeso kwake nokupenda miromo yake akapfeka mhete munzeve make dzeruvara ruchena akapfeka hembe isina maoko neruvara ruchena neruvara rutema akagadzira musoro wake zvakanaka akaisa shedhi akapushira bvudzi rake kumashure akasunga chipomupomu cherudzi rusiri rwebvudzi rake.

Nearby grows a variety of trees including a mango tree with green leaves, alongside flowers with green leaves and pink blossoms near a fence. lessons.title: Chidzidzo 96: Munhukadzi mumwe chete akamira akabata muchiuno...
lessons.shona_text: Munhukadzi mumwe chete akamira akabata muchiuno chake. Ane musoro une bvudzi rakawanda rakasvibira ritema. Maziso ake akapendewa nebhuruu. Muruoko akapfeka zvindarira zvakawanda. Musika wembatatisi unoonekwa mune rima imomo. Vanhu vane mahovhorosi vakagara pasi vachitengesera vakamira uye vakapfekawo zvitsvuku vanofarira basa ravo rekuti vaite mari yekuvapa pundutso. Overhead, two birds perch on four electric power lines attached to a large pole near pawpaw trees.

grammar_notes.title: Giving Commands & Polite Requests ('rima')
grammar_notes.content: Notice the command verb 'rima' in this sentence. In Shona, a direct command to one person (singular) is simply the verb stem ending in '-a'—for example, 'Vhara!' ('Close!'), 'Tora!' ('Take!'), or 'Huya!' ('Come!'). When speaking to more than one person, or when showing polite respect to an adult, you add '-i' to the end, changing '-a' to '-ai' (as in 'Huyai!' = 'Come!' or 'Batai!' = 'Catch/Hold!'). Adding the prefix 'chi-' (as in 'Chiuya' or 'Chigara') means 'Do it right now'.
grammar_notes.rule: Singular Command: Verb stem (-a) [Huya! / Tora!] | Polite or Plural Command: Verb stem + -i (-ai) [Huyai! / Torai!]

lessons.title: Chidzidzo 97: Munhurume wechiAfrica akamira akabata machira ane...
lessons.shona_text: Munhurume wechiAfrica akamira akabata machira ane ruvara rutatu achiratidza kudhekoreta panzvimbo yaakamira. Mbatatisi nhatu dziri pabhodhi rineruvara ruchena idzo dzine ruvara rwakaita goridhe dzirikuratidza hutano. Imwe ihombe dzimwe idiki. Mundiro yemuti iyi muzere madora . Madora aya akakangwa zvakanaka akasanganiswa nematamati nehanyanisi. Ivhu rakawanda rakaunganidzwa rakatsetseka zvinobva zvaita kuti tifungidzire kuti panzvimbo iyi inzvimbo ine zvicherwa zvinocherwa. Ivhu iri ndiro rinocherwa kubva pasi panenge pachicherwa zvicherwa izvi.
lessons.english_translation: An African man stands holding three-coloured cloths to decorate the place where he stands. Three golden, healthy-looking potatoes rest on a white board—one large and the others smaller. A wooden bowl is filled with mopane caterpillars (madora), well-roasted and mixed with tomatoes and onions. Nearby, heaps of excavated soil indicate a mining area where minerals are dug from underground.

grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'ruvara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

cultural_notes.title: Mopane Caterpillars ('Madora'), Irish Potatoes & Zimbabwe's Mineral Wealth
cultural_notes.content: This rich passage connects three icons of Zimbabwean life: golden locally grown potatoes ('mbatatisi'), a wooden bowl ('ndiro yemuti') brimming with protein-rich mopane caterpillars ('madora') pan-roasted with tomatoes and onions, and the mineral-rich soils ('zvicherwa') of the Great Dyke that make mining a cornerstone of Zimbabwe's economy.

lessons.title: Chidzidzo 98: Mushina unoshandiswa kunamirira mitengo kumadziro uye... (Dzokororo 14)
lessons.shona_text: Mushina unoshandiswa kunamirira mitengo kumadziro uye pazvinhu zviri kutengeswa. Marobhotsi anowanikwa mumaguta. Anoita kuti mota dzisabonderane. Vatambi varimunhandare, pane mutambi akamira pagedhi akapfeka zvitema poita vaokeri varikuoneka nechekure. Bhutsu yegumbo rwokurudyi ine mavara akasiyana siyana anosanganisira ruvara rwendarama, rwebhuruu, rweorenji, rwuchena uyewo ruvara rutema.

In a stadium, a goalkeeper in black stands by the goalposts with spectators visible in the distance, alongside a right-foot boot decorated in gold, blue, orange, white, and black.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('wakadzima')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'wakadzima' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('unoshandiswa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'unoshandiswa' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

sections.heading: 3. Cultural Context & Practical Usage
points: Hair Braiding ('Kuruka Bvudzi') & Zimbabwe's Passion for Football ('Nhabvu'): This two-part passage highlights two pillars of contemporary Zimbabwean culture: intricate hairstyling ('kugadzirwa musoro' and twisting braids 'tumabhanzi'), which is both an art form and a social occasion, and football ('nhabvu' or 'bhora')—the country's most popular sport, played passionately in every neighbourhood and stadium..

Neighbourhood Tuckshops ('Matakishopu') & Local Furniture Makers: Across Zimbabwean suburbs, small painted corner shops called 'matakishopu' (tuckshops) provide convenient daily groceries within walking distance of home, while local carpentry workshops and furniture stores craft patterned kitchen cabinets ('makabati') and wardrobes for growing households..

Hand Tools of the Homestead ('Badza, Bhemba, Banga') & Open-Air Market Umbrellas: Notice the four classic tools found in every rural and suburban tool shed in Zimbabwe: the long-handled hoe ('badza') for cultivating, the curved slasher ('bhemba') for clearing tall grass, the utility knife ('banga'), and the grass-cutter—alongside the colourful shade umbrellas ('maamburera') under which women vendors trade at the local market ('pamusika')..

Community Water Points, 'Jojo' Storage Tanks & Backyard Mango Trees: In many Zimbabwean neighbourhoods, solar-powered boreholes ('zvibhorani') feed elevated plastic storage tanks ('Jojo tanks') where residents gather with buckets ('migomo') and containers ('zvigubu') to draw clean water, surrounded by suburban gardens planted with shady green mango trees ('miti yemimango') and bright border flowers..

lessons.title: Chidzidzo 99: Muti mukuru kwazvo une mashizha akasvibira....
lessons.shona_text: Muti mukuru kwazvo une mashizha akasvibira. Muti uyu unoratidza kuti uri kuwana mvura yakakwana nokuti mashizha awo akakura uye akawanda. Pasi pemuti uyu pane ivhu rakatsvuka huye pane twumasora twushoma. Shangu tema dzakavharika kumberi nekumasure. Dzine rudzi rwejombo uye dzine twusimbi twuri kuonekera nechekure twunopenya penya padivi padzo. Dzine tambo dzokusungisa. Nzvimbo iri pakati peguta. Pane vanhu vari kufamba vachienda kumativi akasiyana. Panewo robhoti rinobatsira kuti mota dzifambe zvakanaka. Nechekumberi kune zvivako zviri kubudira, zvivako izvi zvakavakwa zvichikwira mudenga. Nzvimbo iri pedyo nemugwagwa une tara.Ine huswa husina kunyanya kukura.Huswa hwacho hwakaita kutsvukuruka.Panewo miti ine maruva.Maruva acho matsvuku uye mamwe akada kuita pingi.Mashizha emiti iyi ndeegirini.
lessons.english_translation: A very large tree has lush green leaves, showing that it receives plenty of water because its leaves are big and abundant, with red soil and a little grass beneath it. Nearby are closed black boots with shiny metal eyelets and laces. In the city centre, people walk in different directions while traffic lights help cars flow smoothly and high-rise buildings rise ahead. Along a tarred road with short brownish grass stand flowering trees with red and pink blossoms and green leaves.

lessons.title: Chidzidzo 100: Rori huru kwazvo rakamira zvaro. Rori...
lessons.shona_text: Rori huru kwazvo rakamira zvaro. Rori iri rine musoro muchena uye rakanaka zvikuru pakutarisa. Rinoratidza kuti rinogona kutakura zvinhu zvakawanda kwazvo uye rori iri riri panzvimbo inoratidza kuti inzvimbo yekuwedzera mafuta. Shangu dzekurudyi nedzekuruboshwe. Dzine ruvara rwebhuruu neruchena. Dzinoratidza kuti dzakambopfekwa nekuti dzaakukwatanuka. Dzine tambo chena. Shangu idzi dzinogona kupfekwa zvose nevanhurume kana vanhukadzi. Vanhu vakamira padivi pemotokari dzemarudzi rwemakombi mukati meguta nechekumberi kune imba hombe yemudurikanidzwa yakabaka magetsi mukati mayo. Masvingo eGreat Zimbabwe izvi zvinova zvivakwa zvematombo zviri munzvimbo yeMasvingo. Inzvimbo inonyanyawo kushanyirwa nevanhu vachiona mararamiro aiitawo vanhu kare uyewo pane vanhu vari kuratidza kuti vakamira vauya kuzoshanya panzvimbo iyi.
lessons.english_translation: A huge truck is parked; it has a handsome white cab, can carry heavy loads, and is stopped at a fuel station. Nearby are left and right blue-and-white shoes with white laces that can be worn by men or women. In the city, people stand beside commuter minibuses (makombi) with a lit multi-storey building ahead. Finally, the stone walls of Great Zimbabwe in Masvingo are shown—a famous heritage site visited by many people to see how ancestors lived long ago.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('rakamira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'rakamira' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('Rinoratidza')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'Rinoratidza' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

cultural_notes.title: From City 'Makombi' & Freight Trucks to the Stone Walls of Great Zimbabwe
cultural_notes.content: Our final passage brings together modern and ancient Zimbabwe: heavy freight lorries refuelling along the highway, bustling city 'makombi' minibuses beneath illuminated high-rises, and the timeless granite enclosures of Great Zimbabwe ('Masvingo eGreat Zimbabwe'), where visitors from around the world walk in the footsteps of the ancient Shona builders.
